def Target : Prop :=
  ∀ (Fm S₀ S : Type) [LogicalConnective Fm] [LogicalNeutral Fm] [Entailment S₀ Fm] [Entailment S Fm]
    (𝓑 : S₀) (𝓢 : S) [Entailment.Cl 𝓑] [Entailment.Cl 𝓢] (K F : Fm → Fm) (conF : Fm),
    Def1 𝓑 K → Def2 𝓑 K → Def6 𝓑 K → 𝓑 ⪯ 𝓢 →
    Def4 𝓢 K →
    (∃ s, 𝓢 ⊢ K (s 🡘 K (F (∼s)))) →
    (∀ σ, 𝓑 ⊢ conF 🡒 ∼(F σ ⋏ F (∼σ))) →
    (∀ σ, 𝓢 ⊢ K (K σ 🡒 F σ)) →
    𝓢 ⊢ K (∼K conF)

1. (Def1 𝓑 K) For every sentence φ, if 𝓑 proves φ, then 𝓑 proves K φ.
2. (Def2 𝓑 K) For all sentences φ and ψ, 𝓑 proves K (φ 🡒 ψ) 🡒 (K φ 🡒 K ψ).
3. (Def6 𝓑 K) For every sentence φ, 𝓑 proves K φ 🡒 K (K φ).
4. (𝓑 ⪯ 𝓢) Every sentence provable in 𝓑 is provable in 𝓢.
5. (Def4 𝓢 K) For every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K (K φ 🡒 φ).
6. There exists a sentence s such that 𝓢 proves K (s 🡘 K (F (∼s))), where φ 🡘 ψ abbreviates (φ 🡒 ψ) ⋏ (ψ 🡒 φ).
7. For every sentence σ, 𝓑 proves conF 🡒 ∼(F σ ⋏ F (∼σ)).
8. For every sentence σ, 𝓢 proves K (K σ 🡒 F σ).
Then 𝓢 proves K (∼(K conF)).

Nothing else is assumed: in particular, neither 𝓑 nor 𝓢 is required to be consistent; K and F are arbitrary functions on sentences and conF is an arbitrary sentence subject only to hypothesis 7; necessitation (Def1) is assumed only for 𝓑 and not for 𝓢; and reflection K φ 🡒 φ itself (Def3) is not assumed—only its K-prefixed form K (K φ 🡒 φ) in 𝓢 (Def4)."}

translation:
Target is the proposition asserting that for every choice of types Fm (sentences), S₀, and S (proof systems), equipped with the formal logical connectives (🡒, ⋏, ⋎, ∼) and constants (⊤, ⊥) on Fm and entailment relations on Fm for S₀ and S; for every pair of proof systems 𝓑 : S₀ and 𝓢 : S that each prove all classical propositional tautologies in these connectives and are closed under modus ponens; for every pair of arbitrary functions K, F : Fm → Fm; and for every sentence conF : Fm, if all of the following eight hypotheses hold:
1. (Def1 𝓑 K) For every sentence φ, if 𝓑 proves φ, then 𝓑 proves K φ.
2. (Def2 𝓑 K) For all sentences φ and ψ, 𝓑 proves K (φ 🡒 ψ) 🡒 (K φ 🡒 K ψ).
3. (Def6 𝓑 K) For every sentence φ, 𝓑 proves K φ 🡒 K (K φ).
4. (𝓑 ⪯ 𝓢) Every sentence provable in 𝓑 is provable in 𝓢.
5. (Def4 𝓢 K) For every sentence φ, 𝓢 proves K (K φ 🡒 φ).
6. There exists a sentence s such that 𝓢 proves K (s 🡘 K (F (∼s))), where φ 🡘 ψ abbreviates (φ 🡒 ψ) ⋏ (ψ 🡒 φ).
7. For every sentence σ, 𝓑 proves conF 🡒 ∼(F σ ⋏ F (∼σ)).
8. For every sentence σ, 𝓢 proves K (K σ 🡒 F σ).
Then 𝓢 proves K (∼(K conF)).

Nothing else is assumed: in particular, neither 𝓑 nor 𝓢 is required to be consistent; K and F are arbitrary functions on sentences and conF is an arbitrary sentence subject only to hypothesis 7; necessitation (Def1) is assumed only for 𝓑 and not for 𝓢; and reflection K φ 🡒 φ itself (Def3) is not assumed—only its K-prefixed form K (K φ 🡒 φ) in 𝓢 (Def4).

divergences.description: Abstract propositional setting instead of first-order arithmetic with Gödel numbering: Reinhardt states Theorem 6 in a first-order theory of arithmetic extended with B, where q(x) is a formula with one free variable, [s] is a Gödel numeral, ng is a primitive recursive term representing syntactic negation, and axioms are universal closures of formulas. Target abstracts to an arbitrary type Fm with classical propositional connectives and arbitrary functions K, F : Fm → Fm, rendering q(ng[s]) directly as F (∼s) and eliding both arithmetic/quantifiers and the representation step ng[s] = [¬s] (a limitation declared by the author).

Fixed point assumed as an explicit hypothesis rather than derived: in Reinhardt's Theorem 6, the existence of s with T ⊢ B(s ↔ Bq(ng[s])) is not a hypothesis of the theorem but is obtained in the proof from the arithmetical fixed-point (diagonal) theorem for any formula q(x). Target adds (∃ s, 𝓢 ⊢ K (s 🡘 K (F (∼s)))) as a hypothesis, weakening the statement relative to the full arithmetical theorem because the diagonal lemma cannot be proved in the abstract setting.

Abstract characterization of Con q: in the source, Con q is specifically defined as the quantified sentence ∀x¬(q(x) & q(ng(x))) ranging over all numbers. Target cannot express this definition and instead universally quantifies over an arbitrary sentence conF satisfying the sentence-level schema ∀ σ, 𝓑 ⊢ conF 🡒 ∼(F σ ⋏ F (∼σ)); this is an idealization that also slightly generalizes the theorem to any sentence with those instances.

Two-theory split 𝓑 ⪯ 𝓢: Reinhardt works in a single theory T whose axioms are optionally prefixed by B, whereas Target splits into a base theory 𝓑 (closed under necessitation and proving K-distribution, K φ 🡒 K (K φ), and the conF instances) and an extension 𝓢 (proving K (K φ 🡒 φ), the fixed point, and K (K σ 🡒 F σ), without requiring necessitation on 𝓢). This is a harmless strengthening (generalization), as taking 𝓑 = 𝓢 = T recovers the single-theory setting.

Omission of unused axioms from [P-R323]: Target omits the quantifier axiom B∀xP → ∀x Bp (unexpressible without quantifiers and unused in Theorem 6) as well as plain correctness Bp → p (in line with Reinhardt's remark in [P-R328] that only B(Bp → p) is used), and uses only classical propositional logic rather than full first-order logic and arithmetic.

judgement.summary: Target faithfully captures the modal-epistemic structure and conclusion of Reinhardt's Theorem 6, including the exact forms of (B ≤ q), the fixed point, and the weakened reflection axiom B(Bp → p). Its caveats stem from the declared abstraction away from first-order arithmetic, quantifiers, and Gödel coding—most notably taking the diagonal fixed point as an explicit hypothesis rather than deriving it and characterizing Con q only through its sentence-level instances.
